clue.text: Scotch bird whose eggs are toasted

definitions.text: Scotch bird whose eggs are toasted

parts.words: Scotch bird whose eggs are toasted
parts.note: reads as a Scottish game bird, but names the savoury dish of scrambled eggs and anchovy served on toast

explanation.walkthrough: Scotch woodcock is a British savoury: scrambled eggs on toast with anchovies. No bird is involved, which is the trick of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The savoury dish of eggs on toast is named after a game bird, with 'Scotch' in front.

clue.text: Perversion isn't vulgar — it makes a brave show

parts.note: a warp is a twist or perversion
ain't is a vulgar form of isn't

explanation.surface: Perversion may not be crude, yet it puts on a bold display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brave' is a noun: a Native American warrior, who paints his face for battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Face paint worn by warriors going into battle, a brave's display.

clue.text: Alice has lots of trouble with swing

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so these letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: Alice struggles a great deal on the swing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges the nine letters of ALICE and LOTS.
explanation.definitionFit: To move to and fro like a pendulum.

clue.text: (Part of) train

parts.note: read with the bracket, a carriage of a railway train; read without it, the verb to instruct

explanation.walkthrough: The brackets let one clue serve two readings: a railway carriage, and to tutor.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach is a railway carriage, and to coach is to tutor or prepare someone.

clue.text: Ugly ducklings — receiving mail from Scottish lawyers, you say?

indicators.note: 'you say' marks a word that is spoken, so its sound is what counts

parts.note: Writers to the Signet are Scottish solicitors, and their letters bear signets, seals

explanation.surface: Ugly ducklings get letters from Edinburgh solicitors.
explanation.walkthrough: In the fairy tale the ugly duckling grows into a swan, so it was a young swan all along. Writers to the Signet are a society of Scottish lawyers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Andersen's tale the ugly duckling turns out to be a baby swan.

clue.text: One pursues the rascal of course

indicators.note: one thing pursuing another comes after it, so this piece goes last

parts.note: a scamp is a mischievous rascal
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Someone chases a scoundrel, as you would expect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like a throwaway 'naturally', but it is the definition: something served as a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaded prawns are commonly served as a course at dinner.

clue.text: Belts the top general's true, anyhow!

parts.note: C-in-C, commander-in-chief, is the top general

indicators.note: 'anyhow' says the letters of true can come in any order

parts.note: the 's gives an S

explanation.surface: The supreme commander's belts are genuine, at any rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belts' looks like a verb, as in hits; it is the plural noun. C-in-C, commander-in-chief, is a standard crossword abbreviation for a top general.
explanation.definitionFit: A cincture is a girdle or belt, especially round a vestment.

clue.text: This key not being that of the door

definitions.text: This key not being that of the door

parts.words: This key not being that of the door
parts.note: a key that opens no door: a musical key, the one paired with major

explanation.walkthrough: 'key' suggests a door key; the clue says it is not one, leaving the musical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical key based on a scale with a flattened third, the counterpart of major.

clue.text: Pooh-Bah's bribe could be £1 ? Nuts!

indicators.note: 'could be' says these letters may be arranged into another word

parts.note: the pound sign is L, from Latin libra, and 1 is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A bribe of one pound to a corrupt official is crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, Pooh-Bah takes bribes, which he calls being insulted. 'could be' rearranges L, I and NUTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooh-Bah accepts bribes as 'insults' to his pride.

clue.text: Lapels are not quite back

indicators.note: 'not quite' means a word stops one letter short of the whole, losing its final E

parts.note: to reverse is to go back

explanation.surface: Lapels are almost behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Revers are the turned-back edges of a coat front.
explanation.definitionFit: The turned-back facings of a garment, at the lapel or cuff.

clue.text: It has four corners — right!

parts.note: describes a four-cornered shape, and the exclamation hints that the name splits as Latin 'rectus', right, plus angle

explanation.walkthrough: The name itself means 'right angle', and every corner of the shape is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-sided figure whose corners are all right angles.

clue.text: The limit for smart dressers, or squares

definitions.meaning: people dressed as smartly as possible are 'dressed up to the' this
each one is three times three, a square number

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressed up to the nines' is an idiom for the height of smartness.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'to the nines' means to perfection, and the number nine is a square, three times three.

clue.text: Whom some call a heavenly being

definitions.text: Whom some call a heavenly being

indicators.note: 'some' of the words that follow means only part of their letters are taken, a run inside them

explanation.surface: A remark on what many believers call God.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs through 'cALL A Heavenly', and the whole clue also describes it: the Muslim name for God.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabic name for God, used by Muslims, so a heavenly being whom some address in prayer.

clue.text: Oriental reader has a pupil in this college

parts.note: E, east, is what oriental refers to
a lector is a reader, in church or a university
L is a learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: An Eastern lecturer has a student at this college.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the word that comes before 'college': the electoral college that elects a US president, not a teaching institution.
explanation.definitionFit: The body that formally chooses the US president is called the electoral college.

clue.text: Differences of opinion of students' union about cane possibly

indicators.note: the union's letters go about, around, the next piece

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students in Britain

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the letters of cane may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A student union disagrees over corporal punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cane' suggests school punishment, but it is only anagram fodder; 'possibly' rearranges it and 'about' puts the National Union of Students round the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Shades or fine distinctions, the subtle variations between opinions.

clue.text: What may be tipped but not recommended by doctors

definitions.text: What may be tipped but not recommended by doctors

parts.words: What may be tipped but not recommended by doctors
parts.note: something filter-tipped, which medical advice warns against smoking

explanation.walkthrough: 'tipped' suggests a tip or recommendation, which the doctors withhold; it means filter-tipped.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoke with a filter tip, which doctors advise against.

clue.text: Angel could be perhaps beheaded

indicators.note: 'could be' says the remaining letters may be rearranged into a new word
a word beheaded loses its first letter, so perhaps drops its opening P

explanation.surface: Perhaps the angel lost its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' leaves ERHAPS, and 'could be' rearranges those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraph is one of the highest order of angels in Christian tradition.

clue.text: Forecast the rise of one song among publicity men

indicators.note: the reversed piece goes among, inside, the publicity men

parts.note: PROs are public relations officers

indicators.note: in a down clue a rise means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
taken as a song

explanation.surface: Predicting a song's rise up the charts among PR people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the rise of' turns the one and the song upwards together, giving GNOSI, and 'among' sets that inside the public relations officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A prediction of how things, usually an illness, will turn out.

clue.text: Resort for trainee engineers?

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a course is laid on for trainees

explanation.surface: A holiday spot for apprentice engineers?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' wants to be a holiday town; it is a fallback, as in 'have recourse to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something turned to for help, a fallback.

clue.text: Attained by a number on a hill-top

definitions.text: Attained by a number on a hill-top

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another comes after it

parts.note: the top of the word hill is its first letter
eight is a number

explanation.surface: Eight climbers reach the summit of a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: The top letter of hill with EIGHT on it; and the whole clue describes an altitude reached at a summit.
explanation.definitionFit: An elevation or summit is what climbers reach on a hill-top.

clue.text: Form of warfare may be deep under the ocean

definitions.meaning: the dug-in fighting of the First World War is called after its ditches

definitions.text: may be deep under the ocean
definitions.meaning: a long deep gash in the sea floor

explanation.walkthrough: The Mariana is the deepest example on the ocean floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Trench warfare is fought from dug ditches, and an ocean trench is a deep sea-floor gorge.

clue.text: Is bored, terribly, by this order to show one's …

indicators.note: 'terribly' suggests the letters of 'Is bored' are badly mangled

explanation.surface: Bored stiff, someone is ordered to strip down to the clothes in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence runs on into 23 across: the command 'Disrobe!' is an order to show one's underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: To undress, the instruction given to someone to take off their clothes.

clue.text: Daniel adored climbing about the Pole

indicators.note: the turned word goes about, around, the Pole
in a down clue a word climbing reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: N is the North Pole

explanation.surface: Daniel loved going up near the Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns ADORED into DERODA, and 'about' wraps it round N. Daniel Deronda is George Eliot's novel and its hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Deronda is the title hero of George Eliot's last novel.

clue.text: Coarse canvas causes vulgar eructation around Los Angeles

indicators.note: the belch goes around the city's letters

parts.note: a burp is a crude word for a belch

explanation.surface: Rough cloth makes people belch rudely in Los Angeles.
explanation.definitionFit: Hessian, a coarse jute or hemp fabric used for sacks.

clue.text: … foreign articles to the Flower of Durham

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article
der is the German definite article
a flower is a river, something that flows; the Wear flows through Durham

explanation.surface: Continues 21 across: a strip to show one's foreign garments to a Durham river.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis takes up 21 across, 'show one's … underwear'. The River Wear runs through the English city of Durham; 'flower' is a thing that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: The clothes worn beneath outer garments, what disrobing in 21 across would reveal.

clue.text: Rising old skinhead artist

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read upwards, so the pieces run backwards

parts.note: aged means old
the head of the word skin is its first letter

explanation.surface: An elderly skinhead painter is on the up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skinhead' is not a youth: it gives the head of skin. 'Rising' turns S AGED into the painter's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Degas, the French Impressionist painter of ballet dancers.

clue.text: Once fit, but inclination nil

parts.note: a cant is a slope or tilt
nil is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A man once fit now has no inclination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fit' is an old word for a section of a poem, so 'Once fit' means a canto. 'fit' wants to mean healthy; 'Once' marks the archaic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage a 'fit' was a division of a long poem, the same thing as a canto.

clue.text: A rich sort of job For a professor Si

indicators.note: to sort is to arrange, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A lucrative kind of post for an academic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rich' looks like part of a phrase about a well-paid job; with 'A' it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A university professorship is called a chair.

clue.text: Fickle and somewhat flashy ?

definitions.meaning: something that gives out flashes, a lamp or beacon

explanation.walkthrough: 'flashy' seems to mean showy, but here it means giving out flashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Light-hearted means frivolous or changeable, and a lamp is a thing that flashes.

clue.text: Chez Clementine, perhaps, a fool of a solicitor

indicators.note: French for 'at the home of', putting the fool inside the dwelling
'perhaps' says the letters of the home are rearranged

parts.note: in the song 'Oh My Darling, Clementine' she lived 'in a cavern, in a canyon'
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: At Clementine's place, maybe, a lawyer behaved foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solicitor' wants to be a lawyer; it is one who solicits votes or orders. 'perhaps' rearranges Clementine's home to CANVER, and 'Chez' houses the fool inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who goes door to door soliciting votes or custom.

clue.text: Bill gets stuck with job as dispatch clerk?

definitions.meaning: a bill posted on a wall is an advertisement pasted up
someone whose work is to send things off in the mail

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second sense as invented: one who posts letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A printed notice stuck up on a wall, and literally one who sends off mail.

clue.text: This sort of clue is seen in the French game

indicators.note: one piece is seen inside the other, a container

parts.note: le is French for 'the'
this clue is an across clue

explanation.surface: A clue of this kind turns up in a French sport.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to itself: it is printed under Across, so 'this sort of clue' gives ACROSS.
explanation.definitionFit: A team sport played with netted sticks, originally from North America.
